clue.text: Runs off, last to start race

indicators.note: the last letter goes to the start

parts.note: a press runs off copies: it prints them

explanation.surface: An athlete bolts, having come last at the start of a race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runs' and 'race' both pull towards athletics, but 'Runs off' is printing: a press runs off copies.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a sprint is a contest run flat out over a short distance.

clue.text: Part of display dish filled with ten pounds

parts.note: a pie is a dish
X is the Roman numeral for ten, placed inside PIE
L = pounds, from the Latin libra

explanation.surface: A display dish at a buffet stuffed with ten pounds of food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'display dish' looks like one object on show; the break comes after 'display', which belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by part and whole: every screen image is built from these tiny coloured dots.

clue.text: Top executive introducing physical training instructor during hotel's launch

parts.note: an inn is a hotel; its letters wrap the rest

indicators.note: what happens during an event sits inside it

parts.note: chief executive officer
PTI, the military abbreviation, inside CEO to make CEPTIO

explanation.surface: A boss brings in a gym instructor while a hotel is being opened.
explanation.walkthrough: PTI is a British forces abbreviation. The hotel's launch reads as an opening party; 'launch' is the definition, a start.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the inception of a project is its start.

clue.text: Right-winger secures a third of ballot in part of the South West

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it fast

parts.note: a Tory is a British Conservative; the letters open around BA

indicators.note: a third of six letters is two

parts.note: the first third of BALLOT

explanation.surface: A Conservative candidate wins a third of the vote in a West Country seat.
explanation.walkthrough: Torbay is a stretch of the Devon coast in south-west England; the election surface fits it, as it is also a parliamentary seat.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by location: Torbay is a borough on the south Devon coast, in England's South West region.

clue.text: Minus tie, retired accountant's absorbed in book

indicators.note: someone retired has withdrawn, gone back

parts.note: a drawn game is a tie
BK is the abbreviation for book
CA = chartered accountant; reversed to AC and placed inside BK

explanation.surface: Someone without a tie, a retired accountant, is lost in a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minus' reads like 'without', introducing the tie; it is the noun, a negative point.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in noun form: a minus is a disadvantage or snag.

clue.text: With game unfinished, slip saving 90 runs — a remedy for loose openers?

indicators.note: a game left unfinished lacks its end, so DRAUGHTS loses its S

parts.note: DRAUGHTS, the board game (checkers), without its final S
to give someone the slip is to elude them
XC is 90 in Roman numerals, held inside ELUDE
R = runs, the cricket scoring abbreviation

explanation.surface: A cricket match cut short, a fielder at slip saving ninety runs, and a question about shaky opening batsmen.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is cricket throughout: slip is a fielding position and openers are the first two batsmen. The openers that are loose here are doors.
explanation.definitionFit: A playful definition: the strip or padded roll stops cold air getting in round badly fitting doors, the 'openers'.

clue.text: Dislike American model

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for American
a model or version of a product

explanation.surface: Someone takes against an American fashion model.
explanation.walkthrough: 'model' suggests a catwalk, but it is a model of car or phone, a version.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an aversion is a strong feeling against something.

clue.text: Might supporter be victorious after losing heart?

indicators.note: a word's heart is its middle letter, so WIN loses its central I

parts.note: a bra supports
WIN with its central I removed

explanation.surface: A question of whether a football fan could win despite being disheartened.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Might' opens the clue like a modal verb in a question; it is the noun, meaning strength.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean physical strength, muscle power.

clue.text: First off, coach had to restrain Charlie Brown

indicators.note: the first letter comes off, so SCHOOL loses its S

parts.note: to coach is to school; SCHOOL loses its first letter, S
Charlie is C in the NATO alphabet, held inside CHOOL
to have a meal is to eat it

explanation.surface: A sports coach was obliged to hold back a player called Charlie Brown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charlie Brown' reads as the Peanuts character, but the pair splits: Charlie is wordplay and Brown is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by colour: chocolate names a dark shade of brown.

clue.text: Aggravate tree creature trapped in river

parts.note: the Exe is a river in Devon; it wraps the rest
acer is the maple genus
a bat is a creature

explanation.surface: An animal stuck in a river, provoked by a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tree creature' looks like one animal, a tree-dweller, but splits in two. The Exe is a crossword favourite among rivers.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to exacerbate a problem is to make it worse.

clue.text: Unsigned band endlessly performing

indicators.note: without ends at either side, so BAND loses both B and D

parts.note: BAND without its first and last letters
a performer is on, on stage

explanation.surface: A band without a record deal plays on and on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unsigned band' reads as a group with no record contract; the definition is 'Unsigned' alone, as in an anonymous letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An abbreviation: anon, short for anonymous, is printed where no author put a name to the work.

clue.text: Immediately made notes about comrade switching sides, joining British

parts.note: a singer makes musical notes; SANG wraps LAP and B

indicators.note: a word that switches sides has its ends swapped

parts.note: a pal is a comrade; reversed to LAP
B is the abbreviation for British

explanation.surface: Someone jots down notes at once about a comrade who defects to the British side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made notes' suggests writing; the notes are musical. The surface's defection is a reversal.
explanation.definitionFit: A regional use: slap-bang is informal British for at once, right away.

clue.text: One picks up signal or silence on radio?

indicators.note: on the radio you only hear the word, not how it is spelt, so a sound-alike is wanted

parts.note: to censor someone is to silence them

explanation.surface: A question about whether a radio receiver is picking up a transmission or dead air.
explanation.walkthrough: The radio surface makes 'signal' and 'silence' look like broadcast terms, but 'silence' is a verb here, meaning to censor.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by function: a sensor is a device that detects light, heat or movement and responds.

clue.text: Upmarket establishment considered removing carpet

indicators.note: removing takes something away

parts.note: a considered act is a deliberate one
to carpet someone is British slang for giving them a telling-off

explanation.surface: A smart shop thinks about pulling up its carpets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carpet' looks like flooring but is a verb: to be carpeted is to be reprimanded by the boss.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a delicatessen sells fine foods and tends to be pricey.

clue.text: Fugitive's desperate leap across border, about to be picked up

indicators.note: a desperate leap is wild and disordered, so LEAP is rearranged
to go across something is to span it
in a down entry, picking something up lifts it so it reads upwards

parts.note: anagram fodder, split EP…AL around the rest
a hem is a border on cloth
re = about; reversed to ER

explanation.surface: An escaped prisoner makes a wild jump over a frontier, about to be caught.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fugitive' looks like a runaway noun but is the adjective meaning fleeting.
explanation.definitionFit: A literary sense: fugitive as an adjective means fleeting, short-lived.

clue.text: Irregular patrol keeping in charge of torrid area

indicators.note: irregular means not in the usual order, so PATROL is rearranged
to keep something is to hold it

parts.note: anagram fodder, split TROP…AL
IC = in charge

explanation.surface: A band of irregular soldiers patrolling a hot region.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Irregular patrol' reads as guerrilla soldiers; 'Irregular' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by region: the torrid zone is the hot belt between the tropics.

clue.text: Substituting player, United's No 4 — one blows the whistle

parts.note: a substitute comes in for another player
a man is a player in a team

indicators.note: number four in a line of letters is the fourth one

parts.note: the fourth letter of UNITED

explanation.surface: A football substitution for United's number 4, with the referee blowing his whistle.
explanation.walkthrough: The football picture makes the whistle-blower the referee; the person meant tells tales.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by action: an informant tells on others, as a whistle-blower does.

clue.text: Saw waitress tucking into old crust of bread

parts.note: O = old

indicators.note: to tuck into something is to push inside it
a crust is the outside, so only the outer letters of BREAD are used

parts.note: the outer letters of BREAD, wrapped around SERVE
used as a verb, to waitress is to serve at table

explanation.surface: A waitress spotted eating an old crust of bread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'waitress' is a noun turned verb: to waitress is to serve. 'tucking into' looks like eating but means going inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in past tense: to have observed something is to have seen it.

clue.text: Animal on lead comes across perfect place for a tinkle

indicators.note: in an across entry, one thing on another comes after it
to come across something is to span it

parts.note: Pb is the chemical symbol for lead; it goes around HONE
to hone a skill is to perfect it
an ox is an animal

explanation.surface: A dog on its lead finds the ideal spot to relieve itself.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang a tinkle is a phone call ('give me a tinkle'), not a wee. 'lead' is the metal, not a dog lead.
explanation.definitionFit: A regional use: in British slang a tinkle is a phone call, made from a public telephone booth.

clue.text: Quickly went off trifle, wanting sandwiches

indicators.note: a sandwich holds its filling between two outer layers, so the answer sits within the words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Someone lost their appetite for trifle and wanted sandwiches instead.
explanation.walkthrough: The dessert-and-sandwich surface makes 'went off' mean lost a taste for; it is flew off, left in a hurry.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: to fly off is to leave in a hurry.

clue.text: Stand in street, banished from town

indicators.note: to banish is to send away

parts.note: Stafford is the county town of Staffordshire, in the English Midlands
ST = street; removed from the front of STAFFORD

explanation.surface: A protester standing in the street is thrown out of town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stand' is used in the sense of paying for something, as in 'I'll stand you a drink'.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: to stand someone a drink is to pay for it, which needs the means to do so.

clue.text: Clue ultimately simple, retaining good surface

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so take the last letter of CLUE

parts.note: the last letter of CLUE
mere = simple, nothing more than
G = good, placed inside MERE

explanation.surface: A setter's remark that the clue is simple in the end, with a good surface reading.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue talks about its own surface reading; 'surface' is a verb, to come up.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as verbs: both mean to come up from below into view.

clue.text: Moves from the Caribbean, initially being housed in strange area

definitions.note: 'Moves' is plural and RUMBA is singular: the dance is a set of moves.

indicators.note: something housed in a place sits within it

parts.note: rum is British informal for odd or strange

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so take the first letter of BEING

parts.note: first letter of BEING, housed between RUM and A
A = area

explanation.surface: People moving away from the Caribbean first settle in an unfamiliar district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moves from' reads like people relocating; the moves are dance steps from Cuba. 'Rum' fits the Caribbean too.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by origin: the rumba is a dance that began in Cuba.

clue.text: Having gathered airmen, one left at sea?

definitions.text: Having gathered airmen, one left at sea?

indicators.note: at sea means confused, so I and LEFT are rearranged

parts.note: I (one) with LEFT, rearranged and split LIFE…T
the Royal Air Force

explanation.surface: A craft that has picked up downed airmen, one of them left drifting at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: a life raft is left at sea gathering airmen who have ditched.
explanation.definitionFit: An &lit: an inflatable boat set adrift for survivors really does gather up ditched airmen.

clue.text: Upon which kippers may be laid out before breakfast?

definitions.text: Upon which kippers may be laid out before breakfast?

parts.note: surface: smoked herrings; meant: people having a kip, a sleep
surface: set out on a plate for the meal; meant: lying stretched out asleep overnight

explanation.surface: Smoked herrings set out ready to be served at breakfast.
explanation.walkthrough: A kipper is a smoked herring, a British breakfast dish, but 'kip' means sleep, so kippers are sleepers laid out on a bed overnight.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic definition: a futon is a thin mattress bed on which sleepers lie until morning.

clue.text: Trolley's last piece of toast and butter

indicators.note: the last piece is the final letter

parts.note: the last letter of TOAST
a ram is an animal that butts

explanation.surface: The last slice of buttered toast left on a breakfast trolley.
explanation.walkthrough: 'butter' is one that butts, a ram, not the spread.
explanation.definitionFit: An older sense: a trolley or trolleycar is a streetcar running on rails.

clue.text: To bring in Democrat, is any vote spoiled? It's not pleasant to watch

indicators.note: to bring someone in is to take them inside
a spoiled vote is ruined, so IS ANY VOTE is jumbled

parts.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters
D = Democrat

explanation.surface: A question about whether any ballot was spoiled to let a Democrat in, followed by a grim verdict.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Video nasty' was the 1980s British name for a violent horror film on videotape.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by description: a gory horror film on tape is nothing anyone enjoys watching.

clue.text: Overhaul completely turned around unproductive plant

indicators.note: something turned completely faces the other way

parts.note: to overhaul is to redo; reversed to ODER
a lean year is an unproductive one

explanation.surface: A gardener gives a barren shrub a complete overhaul.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unproductive plant' looks like one phrase, but only 'plant' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the oleander is a flowering evergreen shrub.

clue.text: Seeing the onset of digitalisation, money's invested in silver

indicators.note: onset means the beginning, so take the first letter of DIGITALISATION

parts.note: the first letter of DIGITALISATION
Ag is the chemical symbol for silver; it wraps TIN
tin is British slang for money

explanation.surface: With everything going digital, people put their cash into silver.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seeing' is used in the romantic sense: to be seeing someone is to be dating them.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: to be seeing someone is to be going out with them romantically.
